ABSTRACT
The purpose of this study was to take a ﬁrst step toward constructing a developmental and
sex-speciﬁc version of a parametric vocal tract area function model representative of male
and female vocal tracts ranging in age from infancy to 12 years, as well as adult. Anatomic
measurements collected from a large imaging database of male and female children and
adults provided the dataset from which length warping and cross-dimension scaling functions
were derived, and applied to the adult-based vocal tract model to project it backward
along an age continuum. The resulting model was assessed qualitatively by projecting
hypothetical vocal tract shapes onto midsagittal images from the cohort of children, and
quantitatively by comparison of formant frequencies produced by the model to those reported
in the literature. An additional validation of modeled vocal tract shapes was made possible
by comparison to cross-sectional area measurements obtained for children and adults using
acoustic pharyngometry. This initial attempt to generate a sex-speciﬁc developmental vocal
tract model paves a path to study the relation of vocal tract dimensions to documented
prepubertal acoustic diﬀerences.
PACS: 43.70.Bk, 43.70.Aj
2
I. INTRODUCTION1
For purposes of studying acoustic characteristics of speech production, and for generating2
simulated speech sounds, the conﬁguration of the human vocal tract can be represented3
by the variation in cross-sectional area along a curvilinear axis extending from glottis to4
lips. Simplifying complex vocal tract shapes as area functions allows for straightforward5
calculations of resonance frequencies and bandwidths, as well as sound generation based6
on one-dimensional wave propagation algorithms. Over the past few decades, sets of area7
functions corresponding to vowels and consonants produced by speciﬁc talkers have been8
obtained by utilizing various 3D imaging modalities and image analysis techniques (e.g.,9
Baer et al., 1991; Yang and Kasuya, 1994; Narayanan et al, 1995, 1997a, 1997b; Alwan et10
al., 1997; Story et al., 1996,1998, 2001; Story, 2005b; Takemoto et al., 2006). While these11
data sets are valuable contributions to understanding various aspects of speech production,12
they are all based on the vocal tract conﬁgurations of adult talkers, and hence represent13
adult speech. There is a paucity of similar data representing vocal tract shapes produced14
by children as they grow and develop from infancy through puberty. Consequently, it is15
diﬃcult to simulate child-like speech as well as investigate various developmental acoustic16
phenomena that remain unexplained. For example, formant frequencies change very little17
during the ﬁrst two years of life (Buhr, 1980; Gilbert et al, 1997; Kent and Murray, 1982)18
even though increases in vocal tract length suggest they should decrease (Vorperian et al.,19
2005, 2009). There are also reported sex diﬀerences in formant frequencies by age four20
(Perry et al. 2001), despite there being essentially no sex diﬀerences in vocal tract length21
(Fitch and Giedd, 1999; Vorperian et al. 2005, 2009). Questions such as these need to be22
addressed with knowledge of how the vocal tract is conﬁgured during production of speech23
sounds.24
With the exception of area functions reported by Yang and Kasuya (1994) for three25
vowels /i, A, u/ produced by an 11 year old boy, there are, to the authors’ knowledge, no26
reported sets of area functions of vowels or consonants measured for children at any age27
prior to puberty. There is good reason for this absence of area function data: Collection28
of volumetric image sets requires the talker to perform static speech sounds repeatedly,29
typically in supine position, in a medical diagnostic environment that can be intimidating,30
sometimes even to adults. Thus, collecting image sets of this type based on speech sound31
3
production from children would be, in most cases, impractical.32
Medical imaging, such as X-ray, CT, and MRI, however, has been used to secure anatomic33
data on the size and shape of vocal tract structures by either teaming up with other prospec-34
tive imaging studies, such as the anatomic data from MRI reported by Fitch and Giedd35
(1999), or by retrospectively collecting scans of infants, children and adolescents who were36
imaged (many subjects representing a large age range) for various medical reasons using37
strict criteria to exclude cases or diagnoses that alter or aﬀect the clear visualization of38
the anatomic structures that contribute to speech production (Vorperian et al., 1999, 2005,39
2009, 2011; Barbier et al., 2015). Although indispensable for understanding the structural40
development of the speech production mechanism, these data do not provide an indication of41
the actual vocal tract shapes that children conﬁgure to produce speech sounds at successive42
stages of development.43
A typical approach to studying the relation of vocal tract shape to acoustic characteristics44
in children is to generate hypothetical area functions using some type of model based on45
knowledge, however limited, of the anatomic structures at a given age (cf., Lieberman and46
Crelin, 1971; Nordstr¨ om, 1977; Goldstein, 1980; Bo¨ e, 1999; M´ enard et al., 2004, 2009). An47
early attempt was reported by Lieberman and Crelin (1971) who measured cross-sectional48
areas of plaster casts made from newborn infant and adult cadavers. Assuming these to49
approximate neutral area functions (i.e., roughly an /@/), they perturbed them into possible50
conﬁgurations of the vowels/i/, /A/, and /u/. They concluded that, because of the relatively51
short pharyngeal section of the infant vocal tract, infants would not be able to produce52
formant frequencies that present the same degree of acoustic contrast between vowels as53
adults. The suggestion was that a 1:1 ratio of the lengths of the oral cavity to the pharyngeal54
cavity is necessary to allow the vocal tract to take on “two-tube” conﬁgurations that produce55
distinct formant frequencies characterizing the corner vowels in adult speech, whereas this56
ratio has been shown to be roughly 1.5:1 in infants. In more recent publications regarding57
infant, Neanderthal, and nonhuman primate vocalizations, Lieberman (e.g., 2006, 2007,58
2012) has maintained that the ratio of the horizontal and vertical aspects of the vocal tract59
is a primary factor in the emergence and development of human speech production abilities.60
Indeed, based on extensive of analysis of longitudinally-collected midsagittal radiographs of61
children engaged in nonspeech tasks, Lieberman and McCarthy (1999) and Lieberman et. al.62
(2001) showed that a 1:1 ratio is not achieved until about 6-8 years of age. Similar results63
4
were reported by Fitch and Giedd (1999) and Vorperian et al. (2005).64
A diﬀerent approach was reported by Nordstr¨ om (1977) who generated hypothetical area65
functions of infant and adult female vocal tracts by modifying measured adult male area66
functions from Fant (1960). Modiﬁcations consisted of reducing the pharyngeal cavity size,67
both in length and volume. Although calculations of vocal tract resonance frequencies for68
the infant and female area functions were in the direction of observed formant values, they69
did not conﬁrm the formant scaling factors that had been previously proposed by Fant70
(1966; 1975). Nordstr¨ om concluded that children and adult females must use vocal tract71
conﬁgurations that diﬀer in ways that are not captured by simple length and volume scaling72
adjustments.73
Other eﬀorts to generate hypothetical area functions have been based on developing artic-74
ulatory models for which a given set of anatomically-based parameters dictate the positions75
of speech articulators such that they form a speciﬁc vocal tract shape in the midsagittal76
plane. An area function is then obtained by transforming midsagittal cross-distances to77
cross-sectional areas (cf., Heinz and Stevens, 1965; Beautemps et al., 1995). This was the78
approach of Goldstein (1980) who compiled growth curves of 19 structures based on vari-79
ety of published anatomic data, then used curve ﬁts of the data to generate age-dependent80
parameter values for an articulatory model (speciﬁcally, Mermelstein, 1973). The result81
was a model of the vocal tract that could “grow” from infancy to adulthood and produce82
plausible child-like acoustic characteristics. Although not focused on children’s speech per83
se, de Boer (2010) used a highly simpliﬁed version of the Mermelstein (1973) articulatory84
model to show that a roughly 1:1 oral cavity to pharyngeal ratio produced the largest range85
of acoustic contrast between vowels, thus supporting the previously discussed hypothesis86
of Lieberman. Badin et. al. (2014) disputed de Boer’s ﬁndings because of the absence of87
a lip section in his formulation of the articulatory model. An independently-controlled lip88
section, it was argued, would allow for compensation of a wide range of laryngeal heights89
(and hence pharyngeal cavity lengths) to maintain a large [ F1,F 2] vowel space.90
Another series of studies have demonstrated the eﬀects of vocal tract growth on speech91
by modifying the parameters of the Variable Linear Articulatory Model (VLAM) (Bo¨ e and92
Maeda, 1998; M´ enard et al., 2004). The VLAM is based on a midsagittal representation93
of the vocal tract originally developed by Maeda (1979, 1990) in which linear combinations94
of vocal tract shaping components obtained from factor analysis of cineradiographic images95
5
of two adult female talkers (native speakers of French) were used to reconstruct vocal tract96
conﬁgurations. Minimally, the parameters of the model control the shape and position of the97
tongue, lips, jaw, and larynx height, but may also include speciﬁcation of palate height, and98
pharyngeal wall contour (Bo¨ e et al., 2006). The VLAM operates by ﬁrst specifying parameter99
values of the Maeda model in the original adult domain, resulting in a midsagittal vocal100
tract conﬁguration. To transform to a child-like vocal tract, two scaling factors, one for the101
pharynx and another for the oral cavity, are used to impose age-dependent and nonuniform102
modiﬁcations of both the length axis as well as the distance across the tract. The values of103
the two scaling factors across age are based on data and results reported in Goldstein (1980).104
An area function is obtained by converting the midsagittal cross-distances to areas via the105
approach given in Heinz and Stevens (1964), and is assumed to be the same for children106
as adults. Similar in concept to Nordstr¨ om (1977), the notion is that reduction of cross-107
sectional area (or midsagittal cross-distance) is proportionally coincident with contraction108
of the vocal tract length axis. The VLAM has been used extensively to simulate vocal tract109
growth, and has demonstrated hypothetical conﬁgurations that could perhaps be achieved110
by children during speech production (Bo¨ e et al., 2013). By necessity, however, their means111
of validation has been based primarily on comparison of calculated formant frequencies to112
those reported in the literature rather than to actual measurements of vocal tract shapes.113
Essentially the same model has been implemented by Oohashi et al. (2017) in a system114
that maps formant frequencies measured from acoustic recordings of children to hypothetical115
vocal tract shapes. These can be used to show possible diﬀerences in articulatory conﬁg-116
urations for production of a variety of vowels at speciﬁc ages. The Maeda articulatory117
model was also used by Callan et al. (2000) in a study of motor control strategies as the118
vocal tract grows and develops. The parameters of the articulatory model were modiﬁed119
with developmental growth curves of various anatomic structures that had been measured120
from MR images. Coupled with the DIVA neural network model (Guenther, 1998), diﬀerent121
strategies were learned by the model for producing vowels at diﬀerent ages to compensate122
for developmental morphological changes.123
As summarized by de Boer and Fitch (2010), vocal tract models can be roughly catego-124
rized as geometric or statistical. A model such as the one described by Mermelstein (1973)125
is a geometric system of articulatory structures deﬁned by anatomic measurements, whereas126
a model like Maeda’s (1979, 1990) is statistical in the sense that a given vocal tract conﬁgu-127
6
ration is generated by combining shaping patterns that have been derived from some type of128
statistical analysis (e.g., principal component analysis or factor analysis) of articulatory data129
obtained during speech production. Although each type has advantages and disadvantages,130
the use of statistical models (e.g., Maeda, 1979, 1999) to investigate articulatory and acous-131
tic possibilities of the developing human and nonhuman primate vocal tract, particularly132
the VLAM approach, has been criticized on the grounds that it inappropriately reconﬁgures133
statistically-derived shaping patterns for an adult vocal tract to ﬁt the anatomical structure134
of a child (cf. Lieberman, 2012). In the view of de Boer and Fitch (2010), this approach135
suﬀers from “logical circularity” because the key aspects of the adult vocal tract (i.e., the136
ability to produce large discontinuities in cross-section in the pharynx relative to the oral137
cavity) are maintained in the reconﬁguring process, and thus overestimates the abilities of138
a child talker. The suggestion is that the anatomy should deﬁne and constrain a model of139
the child’s vocal tract shape, not be used to modify an already mature one.140
There is clearly no direct path for modeling the vocal tract shape of children. Advances in141
magnetic resonance imaging techniques, along with articulography and ultrasound, continue142
to add to our knowledge of anatomy, tongue conﬁguration, and articulatory movement during143
speech development, but measurement of vocal tract area functions produced by children144
during speech production remains elusive. Thus, development of models must rely, in large145
part, on using documented prepubertal diﬀerences of vocal tract anatomy (e.g., Lieberman146
& McCarthy, 1999; Fitch & Giedd, 1999; Vorperian et al., 2011) and acoustic data (cf.147
summary in Vorperian & Kent, 2007) to inform and validate possible conﬁgurations of the148
vocal tract for children’s production of vowels and consonants. Attempts to build age-149
dependent and sex-speciﬁc vocal tract models are needed in order to explore the possible150
acoustic characteristics and perception of children’s speech.151
The aim of this study was to take a ﬁrst step toward constructing a developmental and152
sex-speciﬁc version of the parametric area function model described in Story (2005a). For153
vowel production, the adult form of this model generates a vocal tract conﬁguration by154
deforming a neutral tract shape with a linear combination of two shaping patterns whose155
contributions are controlled by the amplitudes and polarities of two parameters. Informed156
by anatomic data based on direct measurements from imaging studies of a large cohort of157
children and adults, the model components were warped along their length axis and scaled in158
cross-section to become representative of a male or female child at a given age. This approach159
7
does indeed consist of transforming a statistically-based adult model to one that is child-160
like, but the anatomically-based length warping process generates nonuniform, continuous161
age and sex-dependent scaling functions that modify the cross-dimension of the vocal tract162
such that the pharyngeal portion is attenuated to a greater degree than the oral cavity. That163
is, the adult-like abilities to expand and constrict the back and front portions of the vocal164
tract are considerably altered by processes based on anatomical measurements. In addition,165
the two model parameters that control vocal tract shape have been shown to maintain a166
one-to-one relation with the ﬁrst two acoustic resonances ([fR1,fR2]) of the vocal tract, thus167
the transformation of the model from adult to child will indicate whether the one-to-one168
mapping is retained, and how the vowel space may be expanded, contracted, or deformed169
under those conditions. Modeling the area function directly, rather than in the midsagittal170
plane, is also an advantage because it eliminates the need for converting cross-distances to171
areas (Heinz & Stevens, 1964; Mermelstein, 1973) , an operation that is essentially unknown172
for children’s vocal tracts (cf., McGowan et al. 2012). The resulting model was assessed173
qualitatively by projecting hypothetical vocal tract shapes onto selected midsagittal images174
of children in the cohort, and quantitatively by comparison of formant frequencies produced175
by the model to those reported in the literature. An additional validation of modeled vocal176
tract shapes was made possible by comparison to cross-sectional area measurements obtained177
for children and adults using acoustic pharyngometry.178
The article is arranged such that the area function model is brieﬂy reviewed in Section179
II. Measurement and analysis of anatomic landmarks are presented in Section III, followed180
by the description of a technique for warping the length axis of the vocal tract, and scaling181
the cross-dimensions of the model components based on the anatomic data in Section IV.182
Application of the technique is demonstrated in Section V along with assessment of the183
plausibility of hypothetical area functions generated by the model, and comparison of their184
acoustic resonance frequencies to measured formant values. In most sections, “method” and185
“results” are combined in order maintain the sequential nature required for describing the186
process of transforming the adult model to various stages of child development.187
8
II. AREA FUNCTION MODEL OF THE VOCAL TRACT188
The model of the vocal tract is based on a principal component analysis (PCA) of vowel189
area functions of an adult male talker (Story, 2005a, 2009). The speciﬁc set used to build190
the model for this study were the ten target vowels /i, I, E, æ, 2, A, O, o, U, u/ reported in191
Story et al. (1996). Prior to performing the PCA, each area function was smoothed with a192
3-point moving average ﬁlter and the entry area just above the glottis was set to 0.5 cm 2.193
These preprocessing steps assured that the PCA represented the primary features of the194
overall vocal tract shape and suppressed somewhat the idiosyncrasies of the original talker.195
The processed area functions were then converted to equivalent diameters (see Story, 2005a,196
2009) and the PCA was performed. The vocal tract area function can be speciﬁed as,197
A(x) = π
4 [Ω(x) +q1φ1(x) +q2φ2(x)]2 (1)
where x is the distance from the glottis and Ω( x), φ1(x), and φ2(x) are the mean (neutral)198
vocal tract diameter function and the ﬁrst two principal components (henceforth referred to199
as “modes”as in Story (2005a)), respectively. These three functions, along with the vowel-200
dependent coeﬃcients, q1 and q2, are provided in numerical form in the Appendix. For201
this study, all components of the model and resulting area functions consisted of Nx = 44202
contiguous area elements ordered from the glottal to lip end of the vocal tract. For the adult203
male version, each element has an assumed length of L(i) = 0.4 cm, where i is the element204
number. The value of x corresponding to the ith element is then,205
x(i) =
i∑
z=1
L(z) i = [1,Nx] (2)
and results, in this case, in an overall vocal tract length ofVTL =x(Nx) = 17.6 cm. Because206
L(i) was held constant for all elements, any area function generated with Eqn. 1 will have207
the same VTL, regardless of vowel target. Although this approximation underestimates208
the VTL for some vowels and overestimates it for others, the segment lengths and VTLs209
obtained from the imaging dataset described in the next section are based on a nonspeech210
condition of normal respiration and hence do not provide an indication of vowel-dependent211
length change. Thus, at this stage of model development a constant vocal tract length was212
9
maintained for all vowels.213
The Ω(x), φ1(x), and φ2(x) functions are shown in Fig. 1a. The [q 1,q 2] coeﬃcient pairs214
that reconstruct the original ten area functions are indicated as black dots in Fig. 1b, whereas215
the mesh represents 1600 [ q1,q 2] pairs that span the range of each coeﬃcient dimension.216
Each pair was used to construct a unique area function from which resonance frequencies217
(formants) were determined by calculating a frequency response function based on a trans-218
mission line approach (Sondhi and Schroeter, 1987; Story et al. 2000). This calculation219
included energy losses due to yielding walls, viscosity, heat conduction, and acoustic radia-220
tion at the lips; side branches such the piriform sinuses were not considered for this study.221
The resonance frequencies (f R1,fR2,...) 1 were determined by ﬁnding the peaks in the fre-222
quency response functions with a peak-picking algorithm (Titze et al. 1987). The result is223
the mesh shown in Fig. 1c that represents the acoustic vowel space, in terms of the [fR1,fR2]224
resonances, produced by deformations of the two modes superimposed on the neutral vocal225
tract shape.226
The next sections describe a process by which the components of this model were system-227
atically transformed, based on anatomic data, into a hypothetical vocal tract representative228
of male and female children across an age range from birth to 12 years, as well as to an adult229
female.230
III. ANA TOMIC MEASUREMENTS OF THE VOCAL TRACT231
Transformation of the area function model from adult to child was accomplished with232
developmental anatomic data. Using an extant medical imaging database that was ret-233
rospectively procured by the Vocal Tract Development Laboratory following University of234
Wisconsin-Madison’s Institutional Review Board approval, an imaging dataset of 132 CT235
(i.e., x-ray computed tomography) studies of typically developing individuals was randomly236
selected for the purpose of measuring segment lengths along the vocal tract from the mid-237
sagittal plane. The pediatric cohort of this dataset consisted of 112 (58M; 54F) CT cases238
between the ages birth to 12 years, and the adult cohort consisted of 20 (10M; 10F) CT cases239
ages 18 to 25 years. In all cases, the CT studies were done for various medical conditions240
that did not aﬀect the growth of head and neck structures and were classiﬁed to have a Class241
I bite. All CT studies were acquired using General Electric helical CT scanners, and the242
10
images were stored in Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) format.243
All images were visually inspected to ensure that the entire vocal tract could be visualized.244
Details on image acquisition parameters is provided in Vorperian et al.(2009) and Kelly et245
al. (2017).246
A. Location of points along the vocal tract centerline247
As shown in Fig. 2, image-based measurements were facilitated by initially constructing a248
centerline curve that traverses the midpoints between the inferior (soft tissue) and superior249
(hard and soft tissue) boundaries of the vocal tract wall, extending from the level of the250
true vocal folds (point A) to the intersection of a line drawn tangentially to the anterior251
aspect of the upper (maxillary) and lower (mandibular) lips at the level of the stomion252
(most anterior point of contact between the upper and lower lips; point E). The centerline,253
as well as landmark points along the centerline were placed independently by two trained254
researchers and discrepancies resolved with guidance from a head and neck radiologist prior255
to ﬁnalizing landmark placement for measurements. For additional methodological detail,256
see Vorperian et al. (2009). The curvilinear distance along the centerline, from point A to257
E, is the overall vocal tract length (VTL). Because the analyzed images were not collected258
during production of speech sounds, information is not available regarding possible VTL259
diﬀerences across vowels.260
Each centerline was extracted from the midsagittal image as a matrix of (x,y ) pairs and,261
regardless of actual length, was subsequently resampled to contain 44 rows. The resampling262
was performed for the sake of eﬃciency in relating the measurements to the components of263
the area function model. Allowing point A to serve as the origin, three reference points,264
B, C, and D, indicating the location of selected anatomic reference landmarks along the265
centerline were then determined according to the following speciﬁcations:266
Point B: The point along the centerline that corresponded to the superior extent of267
the epiglottis. Since the epiglottis is a leaf shaped structure, parasagittal slices were268
examined to ensure that its tip was accurately presented in the midsagittal plane.269
Point C: The point located at the intersection of the vocal tract centerline with the270
hard palate/soft palate reference line, an oblique line placed at the beginning of the271
11
hard palate/soft palate overlap, as guided by the nasal septum, and extending to the272
superior border of the anterior tongue. This reference point represents the junction of273
the hard palate and soft palate (HPSP).274
Point D: The point located at the intersection of the the vocal tract centerline and the275
posterior or buccal aspect of the upper and lower lips. This point is an approximate276
indicator of the location of the anterior aspect of the teeth/incisors relative to the277
posterior aspect of the lips.278
Vocal tract centerlines for all 132 cases are shown in Fig. 3, with the males on the left279
and females on the right. The origin for each proﬁle is landmark A (glottis), and the end280
is landmark E (lips). The pediatric cases are plotted with gray lines, and the adults are281
shown with black lines. The measured points B, C, and D are indicated with dots placed282
on each centerline, and the glottis and lips are assumed to be points A and E. Although283
there is observable variation in both the overall shape of the vocal tract centerline and the284
location of each measured point, it is clear that the adult male centerlines demonstrate a285
larger vertical extent than either children or adult females, a well-documented aspect of the286
adult male vocal tract.287
B. Analysis of vocal tract segment lengths288
Based on the ﬁve points (A-E) located along each vocal tract proﬁle, curvilinear distances289
of segments AB, BC, CD, and DE were measured. This was accomplished by accumulating290
the Euclidean distances between successive sample points along the proﬁle, within each seg-291
ment. The measured segments represent approximately the lower pharynx, upper pharynx,292
oral cavity, and lip region. Separated by sex, data points for each segment were averaged293
within 14 age bins deﬁned as 0-0.5 yr, 0.5-1.5 yr, 1.5-2.5 yr, ..., 11.5-12.5 yr, and adult.294
The means and standard deviations for the male and female data are shown in Figs. 4a295
and 4b, respectively, as a function of age where year 0 represents the ﬁrst bin of 0-0.5 yr,296
year 1 represents the second bin of 0.5-1.5 yr and so forth. The gray zone in each plot is297
the age range for which there were no data points. The overall vocal tract length (VTL)298
for the male and female pediatric cases ranged from 8-15.4 cm and 8-15.1 cm respectively.299
The adult male VTLs ranged from 15.8-18.8 with a mean value of 17.6 cm (sd = 0.89 cm),300
12
whereas the range was 14-17.5 cm for females with a mean of 15.6 cm (sd = 1.14 cm).301
To parameterize the growth of both segment length and location of the measured points302
along the vocal tract from 0 years to adult, a double logistic equation (cf. Barbier et al.,303
2015), was ﬁt to each segment of the male and female averaged data sets. The equation,304
which speciﬁes segment length Ls as a function of age χ (in years), was of the form Ls(χ) =305
L1/(1 + exp (−a1(χ−x1))) + (L 2− L1)/(1 + exp (−a2(χ−x2))) where L1 and L2 are amplitude306
values of the two plateaus in the curve, x1 and x2 are age values of the inﬂection points,307
and a1 and a2 are the slopes at the inﬂection points. The parameters of the equation were308
determined for each data set with a nonlinear regression algorithm available in Matlab (i.e.,309
curve ﬁtting toolbox, Mathworks, 2016), and then adjusted slightly to ensure a smooth310
curve. The resulting curve ﬁts are shown as solid lines passing through each set of mean311
segment lengths in Figs. 4a and 4b.312
From Figs. 4a & 4b it can be observed that segment AB for females follows a nearly313
linear path between the ages of 0-12 years, and then plateaus toward the adult segment314
length. In contrast, growth of segment AB for males is more rapid in the 0-2 year range315
and then steadily increases almost linearly to adulthood; at all ages except at 0 years, the316
length of segment AB is larger for males than females. Segment BC, the length of the upper317
pharyngeal portion of the vocal tract, grows rapidly between 0-4 years for males and then318
exhibits essentially linear growth until the adult length is attained, but for females there is319
more curvature throughout the entire age range. This results in smaller BC segment lengths320
for the female from 0-4 years, similar lengths from 4-10 years, and then smaller values than321
the male from 10 years to adulthood. The growth of segment CD, the oral cavity between322
the HPSP junction and incisors, is similarly curved for males and females across all ages,323
showing rapid growth between 0-2 years. The magnitude of the segment, however, is slightly324
larger for females up to 7 years, at which point the male CD segment length becomes larger.325
Segment DE is also fairly similar for both male and female up to about 12 years, and then326
increases more for the male vocal tract as growth progresses toward adulthood. Interestingly,327
the length of BC and CD segments for the male at the earliest age are nearly equal, then328
the length of segment CD increases more rapidly than the length of BC, and maintains a329
greater length until their growth curves cross over each other sometime between 12 years330
and adult. The CD segments for the female, however, are longer than the BC segments331
across the entire age range, but do become nearly equal at the adult stage. The diﬀerence332
13
in the growth curves of the BC and CD segments reﬂect the extensive growth in pharyngeal333
length that takes place during puberty for males, but not females.334
The curves representing the four segments in Figs. 4a and 4b were summed to generate335
overall male and female vocal tract length curves ( VTL ) as a function of age. These are336
plotted in Fig. 4c and indicate that the VTL is nearly equal for males and females at 0337
years, and then there is somewhat more rapid growth for males between 0-3 years. From 3-7338
years the male and female VTL growth follows a similar curve, but the VTL magnitude is339
slightly larger for males. After 7 years, the male and female VTL curves continue to diverge340
as they move toward adult lengths. The VTL values across age and sex are nearly the same341
as reported by Vorperian et al. (2009) and Fitch and Giedd (1999).342
Another way of viewing the curves and the segments they represent is to plot them as343
functions of age and cumulative tract length as shown in Figs. 5a and 5b. The growth of344
each segment can be observed from early age at the bottom to adulthood at the top, and345
overall vocal tract length (VTL) is indicated by the rightmost curve. The maximum VTL346
attained for either males or females, based on this data set, is shown by the thin vertical347
line at the far right of each plot. Overall, after about 4 years, the segments can be seen to348
increase in slightly more linear fashion across age for males than females. In Figs. 5c and349
5d, the length of each segment was normalized to the total vocal tract length at each age.350
In this view, segments can be seen as a proportion of total tract length, regardless of their351
absolute length. The thin, vertical lines on each plot indicate the normalized location of352
the points B, C, and D at the earliest age, so that they can more easily be compared to353
these same locations at later ages. For either male or female, the largest location shift from354
childhood to adulthood is observed for point C, the approximate junction of the hard and355
soft palates, and is indicative of the increased vertical extent of the vocal tract with age.356
IV. TRANSFORMA TION OF THE VOCAL TRACT AREA FUNCTION MODEL357
FROM ADUL T TO CHILD358
The segment lengths and normalized double logistic curves shown in Fig. 5 form the359
basis of the method for warping the length and scaling the cross-sectional dimensions of360
the vocal tract in order to transform the adult-based model described in Section II into361
an age-dependent child-like version. Warping the length axis consists of adjusting the four362
14
segment lengths corresponding to an adult vocal tract such that they become equal to those363
of a child at a target age. An age-dependent scaling function is then derived from the length364
warping process that non-uniformly modiﬁes the cross-dimensions of the Ω(x), φ1(x), and365
φ2(x) components of the model.366
A. Length axis warping367
The ﬁrst step toward warping the length axis is selection of points B, C, and D from368
the normalized segment curves (Fig. 5c & 5d) that are deemed representative of the adult369
vocal tract model. These comprise a vector deﬁned as α = [0 B C D 1], where the 0370
and 1 represent points A and E in the normalized domain. Since the model in Section II371
is based on an adult male, the vector was taken to be the endpoints (age 20) of the male372
growth curves in Fig. 5c. This yields a normalized vector for the adult male vocal tract373
of α = [0 0 .2639 0.5988 0.9180 1], and overall vtlα = 17.6 cm. A second normalized374
location vector, β, is then selected that represents the target age and sex to which the adult375
model will be transformed. As an example, a vector selected from the male set of normalized376
curves (i.e., Fig. 5c) at 4 years of age would be β = [0 0 .2240 0 .5341 0.8952 1] where the377
absolute vocal tract length is vtlβ = 11.6 cm.378
The next step is to generate a normalized length vector, uniformly incremented from379
glottis to lips, that represents the length axis of adult male vocal tract model as,380
Xα(i) =
i∑
z=1
z− 1
Nx− 1 i = [1,Nx] (3)
where Nx = 44 corresponds to the number of elements. This vector is shown schematically381
in Fig. 6a as the upper line of dots, which are equally spaced from 0 (glottis) to 1 (lips). The382
α vector representing the anatomic locations B, C, and D for the adult male are superim-383
posed on Xα(i). The second line of dots in Fig. 6a is a warped length axis, Xβ produced by384
projecting the points in the α vector to the locations speciﬁed in the β vector. This results385
in a non-uniformly incremented length axis where the distance between some points has386
been compressed, and expanded between others. Computationally, this operation was per-387
formed by letting β become a function of α, and then resampling Xα with a piecewise cubic388
interpolation (Fritsch and Carlson, 1980; implemented as the “pchip” algorithm available in389
15
Matlab, Mathworks, 2016) to generate Xβ.390
B. Cross-dimension scaling391
In addition to adjusting the length axis of the vocal tract model to be child-like, the392
cross-dimension from glottis to lips must also be modiﬁed to account for the smaller space393
available to produce expansions and constrictions when the dimensions of the vocal tract are394
reduced. Thus, transforming the adult-based model of Section II requires a scaling function395
that attenuates the Ω(x) function and the modes φ1(x) and φ2(x) appropriately for a child-396
like vocal tract, and is dependent on age and sex. Since the magnitude of the lip opening397
can be similar for children and adults during speech production (e.g., Riely & Smith, 2003;398
Bunton et al., 2013), the scaling function should reduce the cross-dimension more in the399
back portion of the vocal tract than in the front.400
The approach used here is based on the hypothesis that regions along the vocal tract401
length axis that are shortened relative to an adult baseline vocal tract, will also be reduced402
in cross-section by a proportional amount. This can be accomplished by setting an initial403
scale factor to be the ratio of the absolute child vocal tract length (at a target age) to the404
absolute adult tract length, vtlβ/vtlα. The gradients of both the normalized adult and405
child length vectors generated by the length warping process (i.e., the length diﬀerences406
between successive elements in the length vectors) can then be used to weight the initial407
scale factor as a function of distance from the glottis. Thus, a scaling function κ can be408
deﬁned as,409
κ(i) =
( vtlβ
vtlα
)(∇Xβ(i)
∇Xα(i)
)
i = [1,Nx] (4)
where∇Xα(i) and∇Xβ(i) are the gradients of the adult and child (at a target age) length410
vectors, respectively. It is noted that, based on the length warping process in the previous411
section, the adult length vector is uniformly incremented from element to element, so its412
gradient in the denominator could be replaced with the increment value as a constant. The413
gradient notation is used, however, to maintain generality for possible nonuniform versions414
of the adult vector. A ﬁnal operation is smoothing κ(i) with a fourth order FIR ﬁlter set to415
have a normalized cutoﬀ frequency of 0.05. As an example, the scaling function shown in416
Fig. 6b was generated by applying Eqn. 4 (and smoothing ﬁlter) to the length vectors shown417
previously in Fig. 6a (for a 4 year old male) along with the corresponding values of vtlα418
16
and vtlβ. It can be seen that κ(i) gradually increases from a value of 0.54 at the glottis to419
0.86 at the lips, thus reducing the cross-dimension values more in the back portion of the420
vocal tract than in the front.421
C. Age-dependent cross-dimension scaling functions422
Using the adult male vocal tract data as a baseline, the process described in Sections IV.A423
and IV.B was used to generate length warping and scaling functions at one year increments424
from age 0 to 12 years, for both male and female, as well as for an adult female. The initial425
step was to determine the normalized β vectors from the growth curve set representing each426
selected age (see Figs. 4 and 5). These vectors are given in Table I, along with the absolute427
tract length values VTL β. The entry for the adult male is blank because it is the α vector428
that represents the baseline adult male vocal tract (i.e., α = [0 0 .2639 0.5988 0.9180 1],429
and vtlα = 17.6 cm).430
The calculated scaling functions, for male and female, are shown in Figs. 7a and 7b,431
respectively. The even years are indicated by thick lines and denoted with a label at the432
lip end, whereas the odd years are shown as dashed gray lines without labels. As noted433
previously for the 4 year-old male, the scaling functions based on the male measurements434
(Fig. 7a) are fairly ﬂat in the back half of the vocal tract, but increase with steeper slopes435
in the front half. The 0 year scaling function has a more unique shape than the other ages,436
apparently due to the very diﬀerent distribution of segment lengths at the youngest age.437
Each yearly increment increases the magnitude of the scaling function (i.e., less reduction438
of the cross-dimension). The ﬂat scaling function with a constant value of 1.0 for the adult439
male simply reﬂects the fact that it was the baseline from which all other ages, male and440
female, were derived. The female scaling functions in Fig. 7b for ages 2 years to adult all441
slope upward in the back half of the tract beginning with values that are slightly smaller442
those of the male. For the 0 and 1 year cases, scaling functions slope downward in the back443
portion of the tract. All the functions then rise rapidly to about the middle of oral cavity444
where the scaling values are comparable to those calculated for the male data, and then445
either become ﬂat or drop somewhat at the lips. The adult female scaling function has a446
shape that is similar to the others, but the overall values are greater than for all other ages.447
It is noted that if adult female vocal tract measurements were used as the baseline data,448
17
the scaling function for the adult female would be a ﬂat line at 1.0, and all other scaling449
functions, including the adult male, would be shaped according to those data.450
D. T ransformation of the vocal tract model components451
The adult vocal tract area function model described in Section II can now be transformed452
to a child-like version. To demonstrate, the neutral diameter function Ω(i) (see Fig. 1 and453
Table III in Appendix) is plotted in Fig. 8a relative to the normalized length axis Xα (Eqn.454
3). The thin gray line shows the same Ω(i) function, but plotted against the warped axis455
Xβ for the 4 year-old male from Fig. 6a, and shows a shift of the overall shape toward the456
glottis. The eﬀect of the length warping combined with application of the scaling function457
from Fig. 5b is shown by the dashed-dot line ( κ(i)Ω(i) vs Xβ(i)), and results in a large458
reduction of diameter values along the length of the tract, more so in the back half than in459
the front. The transformation is completed by resampling the warped and scaled version of460
the Ω(i) function so that the x-axis contains equidistant intervals. This was carried out with461
the same piecewise cubic interpolation approach used in Section IV.A. Finally, an absolute462
length vector can be generated as,463
x(i) =

Lχ(z) i = [1,Nx] (5)
where Lχ(i) =VTL β/Nx, and represents length of each vocal tract element for a given age464
(Nx = 44 in this study). The adult male Ω(x) and the transformed 4 year-old male version465
are shown in Fig. 8b projected onto their respective absolute length axes.466
Following this same process, the Ω(i), φ1(i), and φ2(i) components of the adult model467
were modiﬁed across age and sex to generate a collection of child-like vocal tract models.468
The results are shown in Fig. 9 where, in all plots, the thick black line represents the original469
adult male model, the thick dashed-dot line is the transformation to the youngest age (0470
years), and all other lines represent the progression through ages 4, 8, and 12 years (other471
years were not shown to maintain clarity in the plots). The additional thick gray line in the472
right column plots represents the transformation to an adult female model. The origin of473
the length axis was oﬀset to be the junction of the hard and soft palates (HPSP, landmark474
“B”) so that the growth in both the front and back portions of the vocal tract could more475
18
easily be seen. Contraction in both length and cross-dimension is apparent for all model476
components, and there are some observable diﬀerences between the male and female versions.477
For example, at the youngest age the neutral function, Ω(x) is slightly larger in the back478
half for the male than the female, but opposite in the front half. The model components,479
Ω(i),φ1(i), and φ2(i), derived for each of the ages shown in Fig. 9 are provided in numerical480

Using the model components derived for each age represented in Fig. 9, the vowel /U/, as482
deﬁned by the [q1,q 2] = [1.68,−1.87] coeﬃcients given in Table II (Appendix), was generated483
with,484
D(i) = Ω(i) +q1φ1(i) +q2φ2(i) (6)
which is a modiﬁed version of Eqn. 1 that produces a diameter function rather than cross-485
sectional areas along the tract length. This was done so that the vocal tract shape could be486
shown in a pseudo-midsagittal view (cf. Story et al., 2001; Story, 2013) in which diameters487
from glottis to lips, are plotted perpendicular to a vocal tract centerline proﬁle 2. The /U/488

that are nearly equal in magnitude.490
The resulting age and sex dependent tract conﬁgurations are shown in Fig. 10 where the491

and female are in the left and right columns, respectively. The β vector points for each age493

otherwise abstract area function onto a more anatomically-relevant perspective indicating498

This perspective shows the age-dependent increase in length and vertical descent of the500
pharyngeal portion of the vocal tract, a lesser increase of the oral cavity length, and the501
nonuniform increase in cross-dimension magnitude. For the 0 year case, the cross-dimension502
of the male oral cavity region is smaller than for the female, whereas the male and female503
conﬁgurations are quite similar for the 4 and 8 year cases, after which the male tract becomes504

V. PLAUSIBILITY OF TRANSFORMED ADUL T-TO-CHILD VOCAL TRACT506
SHAPES507
The plausibility of vocal tract conﬁgurations produced by the transformation process508
was assessed in two ways. First, pseudo-midsagittal plots, similar to those in Fig. 10,509
were projected onto actual midsagittal images of two children. This provides a visual,510
qualitative assessment regarding how well the hypothetical tract shapes appear to “ﬁt” an511
age-matched vocal tract image. The second assessment was based on comparing hypothetical512
area functions to cross-sectional area measurements obtained for children and adults using513
acoustic pharyngometry. Although this technique is an indirect means of measuring area514
values, it provides at least some quantitative validation of the transformation process at the515
level of the area function.516
A. Projection of hypothetical vocal tract shapes onto midsagittal images517
From the image sets used to extract the anatomic measurements, midsagittal sections were518
selected for one male (3 years, 11 months) and one female (1 year, 9 months) participant.519
The speciﬁc images were chosen such that mouth was open and that they represent fairly520
young ages. As an approximate match, pseudo-midsagittal plots like those in Fig. 10 were521
generated based on the transformation process for a hypothetical 4 year-old male and a522
2 year-old female producing a neutral vowel and /i, A, u/. The pseudo-midsagittal plots523
were resized to match the pixel calibration of the midsagittal images and projected onto524
them as shown in Fig. 11. Each vocal tract shape was rotated to align with the appropriate525
anatomical landmarks (points A, B, C, and D), and made to be slightly transparent so that526
the features present in the images can be seen through each hypothetical vocal tract shape.527
Because the images were collected during quiet breathing, the velum is in a lowered position528
for both the male and female. Nonetheless, the projected vowel shapes include regions of529
constriction and expansion that would appear to be possible productions by both the male530
and female in the images. The /i/ vowel is perhaps closest to the shape produced during531
quiet breathing where both the pharyngeal and oral cavity are fairly well matched to the532
images.533
The midsagittal image for the male in the quiet breathing condition was part of a larger534
20
volumetric image set which allowed for measurement of the cross-sectional area within the535
oral and pharyngeal cavities. The black arrows on each of the images in the upper row of536
Fig. 11 point to a location in the pharynx where the area was measured to be 2.0 cm 2, and537
an oral cavity location with a measured area of 0.7 cm 2. In comparison, the area at the538
same pharyngeal location in the model-generated vowel shapes is 0.6, 1.5, 0.15, and 1.3 cm 2539
for the neutral, /i/, /A/, and /u/ vowels, respectively. The 1.5 cm 2 area at this location540
for the projected /i/ tract shape is closest to the 2.0 cm 2 area measured from the image541
set, and accordingly its equivalent diameter is somewhat smaller than the cross-distance of542
the midsagittal image. The areas at the oral cavity location in the model-generated vowel543
shapes are 1.4, 0.1, 3.3, and 0.7 cm 2 for the same four vowels. Here, the area of 0.6 cm 2544
in the projected /u/ vowel is just slightly less than the area measured from the image set,545
and corresponds to near equality of the diameter and midsagittal cross-distance measures.546
The cross-sectional area values produced by the model are clearly in the same range of547
the measured area values from the image set, suggesting that the vocal tract area functions548
generated by the child-like versions of the model are plausible conﬁgurations of these vowels.549
B. Comparison of area functions measured with acoustic pharyngometry to those550
based on the vocal tract growth model551
Transformation of the vocal tract model was also evaluated by comparison to area mea-552
surements based on acoustic pharyngometry, a technique in which acoustic reﬂections emit-553
ted into the vocal tract via a mouthpiece are used to estimate cross-sectional areas along554
the vocal tract length. For a detailed description, see Vorperian et al. (2015); protocols on555
data collection and analysis are available at http://www.waisman.wisc.edu/vocal/resources.556
Although the acoustic pharyngometer generates only indirect measures of cross-sectional557
areas in the oral and pharyngeal portions of the vocal tract during slow exhalation, not558
production of target vowels, it does provide a means of comparing adult vocal tract areas559
to those of children of nearly any age. Vocal tract cross-sectional area reconstructions were560
obtained with the Eccovision acoustic pharyngometer (Sleep Group Solutions, 2009) for an561
adult male and eight children (4 male, 4 female) ranging in age from 4 to 7 years.562
Vocal tract area reconstructions obtained with the Eccovision acoustic pharyngometer are563
shown in Fig. 12, and are denoted in the legends as “APh”. In both panels, the same adult564
21
male vocal tract shape is plotted as the thick black line, whereas the gray dashed lines are the565
4, 5, 6, and 7 year old males in (a) and females of the same ages in (b). The mouthpiece of the566
Eccovision system dictates that the cross-sectional area at the termination of all vocal tract567
shapes (the lingual aspect of the incisors) is approximately 3 cm2, as can be seen in both Fig.568
12a and 12b. Thus, for this ﬁgure it is convenient to plot the area functions with respect to569
the distance from the mouthpiece rather than referenced to the glottis or HPSP. The points570
labeled “OPJ” are the approximate location of the oropharyngeal junction. Additionally,571
because there were no systematic diﬀerences across age within the male and female groups,572
age is not diﬀerentiated by line type in the plots, but the OPJ symbols are unique to each573
age. There are, however, large adult versus child diﬀerences in area along the entire tract574
length, except near the lips as expected due to the inﬂuence of the mouthpiece.575
To test the growth transformation process, the adult area function obtained with the576
Eccovision acoustic pharyngometer was modiﬁed by applying the scaling function, κ(i),577
appropriate for a male and female at an age of 6 years (see Fig. 7), and then compared578
to the actual APh area functions obtained for children (ages 4 to 7). Because the growth579
transformation process was designed to be applied to the vocal tract model in the equivalent580
diameter domain (i.e., prior to the squaring operation in Eqn. 1), the APh area function was581
converted to a diameter function prior to multiplication by κ(i) and then returned back to582
the area domain. In addition, the four anatomic landmarks were not available in the APh583
data, so the length warping could not be applied directly to the adult APh area function.584
Instead, the length axis computed for 6 year olds, male and female, based on the anatomic585
data was used for plotting the transformed APh area functions.586
The solid gray line in each panel of Fig. 12 is the transformation of the adult male APh587
function to a hypothetical version of a 6 year-old child, male in the left panel and female588
in the right. This age was chosen simply as a demonstration; hypothetical area functions589
could be generated at any of the other ages within the range of the APh data and would590
be slightly diﬀerent in cross-sectional area and vocal tract length. The hypothetical, model-591
generated male area function in Fig. 12a is quite similar in overall shape to the other APh592
area functions for the 4-7 year-old males except at the lips (i.e., the growth transformation593
does not account for Eccovision mouthpiece). Along most of the tract length, the cross-594
sectional area passes within the range of the APh child data. This is easily observed within595
the ellipse containing the OPJ points located at about -7 cm from the lips. In Fig. 12b, the596
22
model-generated female area function is, for the most part, similar to the APh area functions597
for 4-7 year females, but is well below one APh area function with area values that exceed598
2.5 cm 2 at a location of about -8 cm from the lips. This belongs to the 5 year old female599
and, relative to the APh data for the other children, seems to be an outlier. Otherwise600
the hypothetical areas are mostly within the range of the APh female data along the entire601
vocal tract, except at the lips. These plots indicate that the growth transformation process602
is capable of projecting an adult vocal tract area function to one that is appropriate for a603
given age.604

A. Comparison of simulated vowel space plots to published formant measurements624
To assess the ability of the age-dependent vocal tract model to produce realistic resonance625

denoted as “AK-mf”. Perry, Ohde and Ashmead (2001) measured the formant frequencies636

In the bottom row of Fig. 13 are the male and female vowel space plots generated for the649

the same as shown previously in Fig. 1c, but is now plotted along with /i, æ, A, u/ formant686
25
data from the studies HGCW, LPN, and PB. Other than two of the /i/ vowels, the model-687
generated mesh contains the formant data; in fact, the ranges of both the mesh and the688
measured formants are nearly the same. The adult female case is similar, where a few of689
the measured vowels are just outside the mesh.690
In summary, the model-generated vowel space meshes for both male and female, contract691
in overall size and shift downward along both the horizontal and vertical axes as age increases692
from bottom to top in Fig. 13. Although this is expected due to the increase in vocal tract693
length that occurs during development, the non-uniform length changes of the four regions694
of the vocal tract, along with corresponding cross-dimension scaling also generate changes695
in the shape of mesh from one age increment to the next, as well as male relative to female.696
For example, the lower left portion of the mesh in the 0 year female case is pulled inward to697
a greater degree than the male, and results in a region extending roughly from [800 , 1600]698
Hz to [1100, 2000] Hz with a higher density of resonance pairs. Similar high density regions699
can be seen in both the male and female meshes at the other ages, but not the adult stage.700
This eﬀect is presumably due to the interaction of the length-warping and scaling process701
with the idiosyncrasies of the particular vocal tract on which the model is based.702
B. Simulated vowels based on the length-warped and scaled vocal tract model703
A simulated vowel was produced based on each of the area functions corresponding to the704
solid black dots in each model-generated mesh, male and female, of Fig. 13. These represent705
the coeﬃcients of the /i, æ, A, u/ vowels in Table A.I (an example of these vocal tract shapes706
for a 4 year-old male were shown in the top row of Fig. 11). The simulations were produced707
with the TubeTalker airway modulation model (Story, 2013), a speech simulator whose voice708
source and vocal tract parameters can be scaled to be appropriate for various ages. Although709
the details of TubeTalker have been reported elsewhere and are beyond the scope this article,710
it is noted that the voice source is a kinematic model of the medial surfaces of the vocal711
folds whose frequency of vibration can be precisely speciﬁed. For these synthetic vowels, the712
fundamental frequency (fo) for each vowel was set to rise and fall around a nominal value713
that was age dependent based on data reported by Eguchi and Hirsh (1968, Table II, p.714
24). The fo values are the same for males and females up to age 8 years, and then became715
sex-speciﬁc. The duration of each vowel is 0.5 seconds. Each sample has been low-pass716
26
ﬁltered with a cutoﬀ frequency of 6000 Hz to preserve only the portion of the spectrum that717
can be represented by one-dimensional wave propagation.718
The vowels are presented for listening in two audio ﬁles, Mm. 1 and Mm. 2, where the ﬁrst719
represents the male vocal tract models and the second ﬁle represents the female vocal tract720
models. Each audio ﬁle arranged such that the /i, æ, A, u/ vowels at a given age are played in721
successive blocks separated by a narrator’s voice announcing each age. These audio samples722
are made available simply to provide an informal experiential means of demonstrating the723
output of the age-dependent vocal tract model.724

VII. DISCUSSION728
The length warping and cross-dimension scaling process developed in this study is essen-729
tially a reverse-growth model of the vocal tract. That is, a model that projects an adult730
vocal tract “backward” in time to a younger age while taking into account prepubertal731
sex-diﬀerences in vocal tract morphology. The results indicate that the model produces732
reasonable child-like vocal tract shapes and vowel spaces, providing support for using it as733
a tool to explore characteristics of speech development.734
The plausibility of vocal tract conﬁgurations generated for various vowels was demon-735
strated by direct comparison to midsagittal images obtained of children in a quiet breathing736
condition. In a qualitative sense, the expansions and constrictions that characterize the set737
of model-generated vowels can be seen to “ﬁt” into the pharyngeal and oral cavity spaces738
exhibited in images of real children. Cross-sectional area measurements based on one set739
of images were also shown to be well aligned with areas produced by the model. This was740
by no means an exhaustive test, but does demonstrate that the warping and scaling pro-741
cess transforms an adult vocal tract model to one that can be considered “child-like” with742
regard to anatomic constraints. Speciﬁcally, the dependence of the cross-dimension scaling743
on the warping of the vocal tract length axis non-uniformly attenuates the epilaryngeal and744
pharyngeal regions of the vocal tract model relative to the oral cavity and lip regions. This745
27
limits the magnitude of possible expansions and constrictions in back half of the vocal tract746
to a greater degree than in the front half, eﬀectively attenuating some of the adult-like747
degrees of freedom for shaping the tract. Additional support was provided by vocal tract748
area measurements obtained with an acoustic pharyngometer (APh). It was shown that an749
adult male APh area function could be transformed, by application of the male and female750
cross-dimension scaling functions, to child-like versions (male and female) comprised of area751
values similar to those of the APh area functions obtained from 4-7 year-old children.752
Plausibility of the vocal tract model was also established by comparison of the model-753
generated vowel space plots (f R2 vs fR1) across the ages 0-12 years and adult, to formant754
data reported in the literature. With the exception of the youngest age, the [f R1,fR2]755
ranges of the modeled vowel spaces were large enough to contain most of the [ F1,F 2] data756
points at each age for both male and female. The vowel spaces could likely be expanded to757
encompass all of the formant data by implementing variable vocal tract length to account758
for actions such as lip protrusion and retraction rather maintaining a constant value for area759
function reconstructions (Mokhtari et al. 2007; Story, 2009). It is also important to note760
that the child-like and adult female versions of the vocal tract model were derived from a761
particular adult male vocal tract (i.e., Story et al, 1996). Any speaker-speciﬁc aspects of762
the original vocal tract model will have an eﬀect on the characteristics of the vowel space763
meshes at each age, but if the model were based on a set of area functions obtained from a764
diﬀerent talker (e.g., Story, 2005b), somewhat diﬀerent vocal tract conﬁgurations and vowel765
spaces would likely be generated. Furthermore, the cognitive and motor control inﬂuences766
of the original adult talker are, to some degree, also embedded in the model and projected767
backward in time. Thus, the derived area function models generated by the transformation768
process do indeed produce possible vocal tract conﬁgurations, but they are dependent on a769
level of cognitive and motor development that may not be fully developed at a given age. In770
addition, acoustic sidebranches such as the piriform sinuses and trachea were not present in771
the calculations of resonance frequencies, but if included would potentially have the eﬀect772
of shifting the main vocal tract resonances either up or down in frequency depending on the773
degree of coupling, location and size of the sidebranch structure, and conﬁguration of the774
vocal tract itself (cf., Dang and Honda, 1997; Stevens, 2000; Pruthi et al., 2007; Honda et775
al., 2010; Delvaux and Howard, 2014; Vampola et al., 2015). Investigation of the eﬀect of776
sidebranch coupling on resonance frequencies and bandwidths of small vocal tracts is one of777
28
the next steps needed to better understand the acoustic characteristics of children’s speech778
production.779
The acoustic assessment of the vocal tract models in this study was limited to only the780
ﬁrst two resonances, fR1 and fR2, to maintain focus on the one-to-one mapping that exists781
between them and the components of the vocal tract model. Higher frequency resonances782
exist, however, for any given area function and are readily available from frequency response783
calculations. The simulated samples provided in the multimedia ﬁles contain the full spec-784
trum of resonances up to the imposed 6000 Hz cutoﬀ frequency. The eﬀect of vocal tract785
morphology on the third and fourth resonances will be important to understand as well, and786
may reveal sex and age dependencies that occur during development. The standing wave787
pattern for higher frequency resonances is more complex though, and may require modeling788
techniques that explore the acoustic sensitivity of vocal tract conﬁgurations (Story, 2006;789
Adachi et al., 2007) and the relation of upper resonances to the voice source (Kitamura et790
al., 2006). Additionally, there are developmental diﬀerences between males and females not791
only in vocal tract morphology but also other aspects of development that may aﬀect the792
acoustic characteristics of speech.793
The approach described in this study for transforming an adult vocal tract model to one794
that represents younger ages, both male and female, is similar to some previous modeling795
studies in that a statistical model was used to represent the tract conﬁguration, and warping796
of the length axis was associated with cross-dimension scaling. It is diﬀerent in several ways,797
however. For example, the VLAM approach (M´ enard et al., 2004; Oohashi et al., 2017) relies798
on a single scale factor in the lower pharynx, another in the oral cavity, and an interpolation799
between them to scale the midsagittal cross-distances according to age (but not sex). In800
contrast, the scaling functions derived in this study from new measurements of anatomic801
landmarks are continuous, nonuniform functions extending from glottis to lips, and are802
dependent on both age and sex. They can be applied directly to the three components of803
the adult-based area function model to generate new versions of the model representative804
of males or females at given ages. These are provided in Tables III and IV for the ages 0,805
4, 8, and 12 years and adult, and can be easily used in combination with Eqn. 1 and the806
coeﬃcients in Table II or the coeﬃcient grid in Fig. 1b, to generate a wide range vocal tract807
area functions at each of the respective ages. Modeling the vocal tract shape directly at the808
level of the area function rather than the midsagittal plane is also an advantage because809
29
it eliminates the need to transform midsagittal cross-distances to areas (Heinz & Stevens,810
1964; Mermelstein, 1973). In addition, even though all child-like and adult female versions811
of the model in this study were derived from the vocal tract structure of a speciﬁc adult812
male (Story et al., 1996), alternative versions, or entirely new “families,” could be easily813
generated based on area functions measured for other talkers. For example, Story (2005b)814
reported sets of 11 vowel area functions of three adult males and three adult females, any of815
which could serve as the initial vocal tract model from which child-like versions are derived.816
Another advantage is that, regardless of age or sex, the vocal tract model requires speci-817
ﬁcation of only two parameters, the q1 andq2 coeﬃcients in Eqn. 1 (also, Fig. 1b and Table818
II), to generate an area function for a vowel. Importantly, these two model parameters819
map in a one-to-one fashion to the ﬁrst two resonance frequencies, or formants, of the vocal820
tract, and maintain this mapping across the age range examined here. An application of this821
relation is that it allows for mapping formant tracks extracted from an audio recording of a822
child’s utterance to a sequence of vocal tract area functions indicating the time-dependence823
of the vocal tract conﬁguration. An example is shown in Fig. 14a where an [F1,F 2] trajectory824
measured from a four year-old male talker’s production of the target word “Iowa” (Bunton825
& Story, 2016) is superimposed on the vowel space generated by the four-year old male vocal826
tract model (i.e., from Fig. 13). Based on the proximity of points along the trajectory to827
those in the vowel space mesh, the corresponding trajectory in the [ q1,q 2] coeﬃcient space828
is determined (see Fig. 1b) and used in conjunction with Eqn. 1 to produce a time-varying829
area function. The vocal tract shapes for the word “Iowa” spoken by the four-year old male830
are shown in pseudo-midsagittal form in Fig. 14b. By coupling this sequence to the same831
type of voice source used to generate the vowel samples, a simulation of the word can be832
produced. It is available for listening in the audio ﬁle Mm. 3.833
Mm. 3. Audio file. This is a file of type mp3 (400 Kb)834
835
The capability of relating formants measured from vowel-like utterances (i.e., vowels and836
vowel-to-vowel transitions) of a child at a given age and sex, to time-varying vocal tract837
shapes, as well as to simulations of the original utterances, provides new opportunities for838
investigating aspects of the production and perception of some types of speech sounds during839
development. Variability of formant trajectories, for example, could be related to vocal tract840
30
shape variability relative to age or sex. This may oﬀer some insight into the timing of vocal841
tract movements relative to males versus females or across an age range. Some aspects of842
speech disorders could also be studied by either mapping formants extracted from vowel-843
like productions of disordered speech to vocal tract shapes, or by modifying simulations844
of typically developing children to become disordered. Simulations such as these might be845
used as stimuli for perceptual experiments in which listeners’ responses could be related846
to systematic modiﬁcations of both the spatial and temporal aspects of the vocal tract847
conﬁguration.848
VIII. CONCLUSION849
This study was a ﬁrst step toward constructing a developmental and sex-speciﬁc version850
of a parametric area function model. A method was developed that utilizes CT-based851
measurements of age and sex speciﬁc anatomic landmarks within the vocal tract to transform852
an adult model to one that represents a hypothetical male or female child at a target age.853
Speciﬁcally, locations of glottis, superior point of the epiglottis, junction of the hard and soft854
palates, posterior or buccal aspect of the upper and lower lips, and the anterior aspect of the855
lips, form a 5-element vector that dictates how the length axis of the adult vocal tract must856
be warped to become child-like for given age and sex. The length warped vocal tract axis was857
then used to determine age-dependent cross-dimension scaling functions that nonuniformly858
attenuate the components of the vocal tract model. The plausibility of vocal tract shapes859
generated by the age-transformed versions of the model was assessed by 1) comparing them860
to midsagittal images obtained from children in a quiet breathing condition, 2) applying861
the transformation to adult APh area functions and comparing the output to APh area862
functions measured for children, and 3) by comparing model-generated vowel space plots863
to measured formant data. These assessments indicated that the vocal tract model can be864
transformed to be reasonably child-like. The results of this study provide a tool that may865
be used to provide insights regarding the possibilities of sound production by small vocal866
tracts, which can facilitate understanding actual vowel production as well as studies of the867
perception of child-like vowel utterances.868

for reconstructing a proﬁle at any target age within the age continuum.898
